extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of comparative government and political theory (general educated readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic criteria and normative observations for judging the institution of the presidency and the qualities/selection of presidents in a democratic republic. Covers institutional checks, electoral effects, social symbolism, candidate selection incentives, and desirable personal traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of "one-man power" / tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: The fear that a President repeatedly chosen would become dangerous to republican institutions (the so-called 'one man power').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why in America this danger is limited (no standing army, inability to create one, Congress can stop supplies, independent States as centres of resistance) and that only in conditions bordering on civil war, or by appealing to the people against Congress, could a President become formidable. Use this to assess the realistic risk of executive usurpation: consider military capacity, popular mobilization, congressional checks, and state resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: President's capacity to influence public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The President has a position of immense dignity, an unrivalled platform from which to impress his ideas (if he has any) upon the people.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the office's persuasive and agenda-setting power: charisma, media presence, and ability to 'force upon [the country's] attention questions which Congress may be neglecting.' Consider whether the holder uses this platform constructively or merely for partisan ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambition-stimulus of the office and its effect on statesmanship
rubrics_metrics.description: In a country without hereditary throne, the presidency 'offers too great a stimulus to ambition' and tempts prominent statesmen to avoid making enemies or to court every section of their party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how electoral incentives distort long-term consistency and willingness to make necessary enemies. Look for evidence of short-term vote-seeking, patronage use to conciliate politicians, and avoidance of principled stands due to presidential ambition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Election frequency and campaign-induced turmoil/cost
rubrics_metrics.description: The presidential election, occurring once in four years, throws the country into months of turmoil; if no serious issues exist, issues are created and much money and business disruption result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to judge the social and economic costs of regular campaigns: duration of campaign season, disturbance to business/finance, and whether the educational value offsets costs. Compare to other systems with shorter or less frequent campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discontinuity of policy and administrative turnover
rubrics_metrics.description: Regularly recurring elections produce discontinuity: new Presidents (even from same party) nominate new cabinets, replace inferior offices, and may change policy; this disrupts continuity of administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess administrative stability across administrations: turnover rates in executive departments, loss of institutional memory, and special mitigation (e.g., Senate cooperation in foreign policy). Consider whether this discontinuity harms long-term policy implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of re-eligibility / term limits on presidential behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Being re-eligible has operated unfavourably: Presidents may play for re-nomination by pandering or using patronage; in second terms they may lack motives to regard national interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how term structure (re-eligibility, term limits, possibility of non-consecutive terms) shapes incentives: propensity to pander, prioritize short-term gains, or shirk national interest once re-election is impossible. The text notes proposals (e.g., six years non-eligible) and trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lame-duck (outgoing President) weakness
rubrics_metrics.description: An outgoing President, during the months after his successor is chosen, 'declines... to take any new departure' except in extreme necessity and therefore is a weak President.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the scope for effective action in lame-duck periods and the institutional/constitutional consequences. Consider the strategic timing of major initiatives and the diminished capacity of outgoing executives, especially when successor is of opposite party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vulnerability of electoral outcomes to disputes and fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: The result of an election may be doubtful not from equality of votes but from disputes as to validity of votes reported from States — charges of fraud or force (example: 1876).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess electoral integrity: laws addressing disputed returns (e.g., 1887 legislation cited), susceptibility to fraudulent returns, mechanisms for adjudication, and potential for popular unrest if perceived unfairness coincides with high passions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive as effective administrator of internal business
rubrics_metrics.description: Despite defects, 'the presidential office... has, for more than a century, carried on the internal administrative business of the nation with due efficiency.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure administrative performance: ability to keep machinery working when Congress is distracted, selecting and supervising subordinates, and sustaining internal administration. Use this to balance criticisms against demonstrated managerial competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility to exercise extraordinary authority in crises
rubrics_metrics.description: At times the President 'has courageously ventured on stretches of authority, held at the time to be doubtfully constitutional, yet necessary,' e.g., Jefferson's Louisiana purchase, Lincoln's emancipation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the institutional capacity for decisive crisis action: extent of constitutional ambiguity exploited in emergencies, retrospective judgment of necessity versus legality, and the risks/benefits of expansive emergency powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional checks preventing a slide to monarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: Several structural limits: no standing army, Congress can stop supplies, no aristocracy to rally round him, States provide centres of resistance — making overthrow of the Constitution hard to imagine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these checklist items to evaluate resilience of republican institutions: military control, legislative purse power, existence of competing centres of authority, and social/political barriers to personal rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social character and ceremonial modesty of the presidency
rubrics_metrics.description: Socially the American presidency is admired: 'the President is simply the first citizen... depending for his dignity on no title... no official dress... his residence... has the air of a large suburban villa rather than of a palace.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess symbolic and ceremonial aspects: degree of ostentation, public deference vs servility, presidential remuneration and expectations, and social role of the President's spouse (examples: Mrs Hayes' temperance advocacy). Consider how social modesty affects legitimacy and public connection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elections as a periodic national review and civic renewal
rubrics_metrics.description: The election is 'a solemn periodical appeal to the nation to review its condition... It stirs and rouses the nation... a direct expression of the will' and sometimes a turning-point in history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the civic functions of presidential elections: whether they provoke national reflection, clarify issues, renew civic duty, and sometimes effect major historical change. Contrast instrumental costs of campaigning with these civic gains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Why great men are often not chosen (talent pool and institutional incentives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Several explanations: smaller proportion of first-rate ability drawn into American politics; methods/habits of Congress give fewer opportunities for personal distinction; eminent men make more enemies; party organisation and loyalty favour safe, mediocre candidates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as a multi-part diagnostic for candidate quality: (a) socio-economic opportunities divert talent from politics; (b) congressional/political structures limit modes of distinction; (c) prominent figures attract inimical scrutiny; (d) party leaders prefer candidates who minimize intra-party losses. Apply each sub-factor when analyzing candidate selection dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candidate selection considerations: geography, section, religion, war service, and electability
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief consideration in selection is the amount of support available from States/sections: large or doubtful States preferred; sectional balance matters; other disqualifiers include Roman Catholicism, avowed disbelief in Christianity (in that period), and service in war could be an advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess electability factors beyond personal merit: sectional/State arithmetic, 'safe' vs 'doubtful' States, religious or cultural acceptability, military service prestige, and local patronage incentives. Use these to explain why parties choose particular nominees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential personal qualities for the President
rubrics_metrics.description: 'His main duties are to be prompt and firm in securing the due execution of the laws and maintaining the public peace, careful and upright in the choice of the executive officials of the country... Firmness, common sense, and most of all, honesty, an honesty above all suspicion of personal interest, are the qualities which the country chiefly needs.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these traits as normative evaluative criteria for any presidential candidate or office-holder: administrative competence, firmness, practical judgment, and unimpeachable integrity. Weigh them above eloquence, profundity, or high culture for ordinary governance tasks.
